title: L3 · Biochemistry & Cell Membrane
subtitle: Inorganic and organic compounds, the membrane, transport

lines.text: **Inorganic** compounds are small, usually ionic, and have no carbon.
Water, salts, acids, bases and buffers.
**Organic** compounds are large, covalent, and contain **carbon**.
Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids and ATP.
Water is about two thirds of body weight.
Polar covalent bonds hold it together.
It is the **universal solvent**.
It lubricates, cushions, regulates temperature and transports.
A **salt** comes from an exchange reaction between an acid and a base.
In water, salts release ions.
An **electrolyte** releases ions and conducts electric current.
Salts, acids and bases are all electrolytes.
An **acid** donates H⁺. It is sour, with pH below 7.
A **base** donates OH⁻. It is bitter and slippery, with pH above 7.
The **pH** scale runs from 0 to 14. Seven is neutral.
Blood pH is **7.35 to 7.45**, slightly basic.
**Buffers** resist sudden changes in pH.
Carbohydrates are the body's preferred energy source.
**Monosaccharides** are single sugars: glucose, fructose, galactose.
**Disaccharides** are two sugars joined by dehydration synthesis.
Sucrose is glucose plus fructose. Lactose is glucose plus galactose.
Polysaccharides are long chains. Plants store starch.
Animals store **glycogen** in the liver and skeletal muscle.
**Triglycerides** cushion, insulate and store energy.
Fat stores twice the energy per gram of carbs, but carbs are preferred.
**Phospholipids** have a water-loving head and water-fearing tails.
They are the main part of every cell membrane.
**Cholesterol** holds membranes together and is used to make hormones.
Proteins are **amino acids** joined by **peptide bonds**. There are 20 amino acids.
Bob Helps To Catch Sam's Iguana Early.
Buffers. Hormones. Transport. Contractile. Structural. Immunoglobulins. Enzymes.
Most protein names end in i n. Enzymes end in a s e.
An **enzyme** is a catalyst.
It lowers the **activation energy** a reaction needs.
The enzyme itself is unchanged by the reaction.
Nucleic acids are the largest molecules in the body.
They are built from **nucleotides**: phosphate, sugar and a base.
**DNA** is double stranded. Its bases are A, T, G and C.
**RNA** is single stranded. It uses U instead of T.
Hydrogen bonds pair A with T, and G with C.
**ATP** is adenosine triphosphate.
It is ribose, adenine and three phosphates.
Breaking the last phosphate bond releases energy.
That is **hydrolysis**: ATP becomes **ADP** plus phosphate plus energy.
ATP powers every activity in the body.
The body has about 35 trillion cells.
The **cell membrane** is the skin of the cell.
The **cytoplasm** is the guts: cytosol, organelles and inclusions.
The **nucleus** is the command center.
The membrane follows the **fluid mosaic** model. Its parts move freely.
A **phospholipid bilayer** forms the base.
**Integral proteins** span the membrane. Peripheral proteins touch one side.
Only integral proteins form channels.
Membrane sugars help with recognition and blood typing.
Cholesterol gives flexible rigidity.
Passive transport uses no ATP.
**Diffusion** moves from high to low concentration.
**Osmosis** is the diffusion of water.
**Facilitated diffusion** needs a carrier. Insulin helps glucose get in.
**Filtration** pushes particles through tiny holes, driven by blood pressure or gravity.
**Isotonic**: equal solutes inside and out. The cell stays the same.
**Hypotonic**: fewer solutes outside. Water moves in, and the cell can burst. That is hemolysis.
**Hypertonic**: more solutes outside. Water moves out, and the cell shrinks. That is crenation.
Active transport uses ATP.
**Endocytosis** brings things in. Phagocytosis is eating. Pinocytosis is drinking.
**Exocytosis** sends things out, like hormones and neurotransmitters.
An ATP-driven carrier moves things against the gradient.
The **sodium-potassium pump** is the example. You'll see it again in muscle.
